narrative:
FIRST WARN FORECAST
Monday, August 31, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

HEAT ADVISORY THROUGH FRIDAY

August is going out hot, and September is apparently planning to pick up right where it left off.

A Heat Advisory is now in effect for the entire First Warn Weather coverage area through Friday as a prolonged stretch of late-summer heat settles across Missouri and Illinois. Afternoon temperatures will repeatedly climb into the upper 90s, with a few locations potentially touching 100 degrees. Daily heat index values will generally peak around 100 degrees, with the possibility of even higher values later this week.

This is not just about one exceptionally hot afternoon. The bigger concern is the duration. We are looking at several consecutive days of significant heat with very little change through the end of the work week.

MONDAY WILL BE ONE OF OUR HOTTEST DAYS THIS SUMMER

A large ridge of high pressure has expanded across much of the eastern two-thirds of the country, while surface high pressure remains anchored across the Southeast.

That puts Missouri and Illinois in persistent south-to-southwest flow, which continues transporting very warm air into the region.

Temperatures Monday afternoon will climb into the upper 90s across much of central Missouri, the St. Louis metro, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois. A few locations could reach the 100-degree mark.

Southwest winds will actually help turn the heat up another notch, particularly across Missouri.

As air travels off the higher terrain of the Ozark Plateau and descends toward central and east-central Missouri, it warms and dries. This downsloping effect can add a couple of degrees to our afternoon temperatures.

That is one reason actual air temperatures may get awfully close to 100 degrees in some locations.

Humidity will be somewhat lower than during some of the oppressive heat waves we experienced earlier this summer. Dewpoints should generally remain in the middle to upper 60s today.

But when the thermometer reads 97, 98, or 99 degrees, lower humidity only helps so much.

Heat index values will still hover around 100 degrees this afternoon.

TUESDAY: REPEAT

There really is not much difference between Monday and Tuesday.

The ridge remains firmly in place, southwest winds continue, and another afternoon of widespread upper 90s is expected.

A few locations could again reach 100 degrees.

Heat index values will once again climb to around 100 degrees during the hottest portion of the afternoon.

This is where heat safety becomes increasingly important. The human body handles one hot afternoon differently than it handles four or five consecutive days of heat.

The effects can accumulate, especially for people who work outdoors, older adults, young children, people without reliable air conditioning, and pets.

Take the Heat Advisory seriously even if the heat index does not reach some of the extreme numbers we saw earlier this summer.

THE HEAT STICKS AROUND ALL WEEK

Unfortunately, there is no meaningful break showing up Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday.

The upper-level ridge may actually strengthen toward the end of the work week, keeping the hottest air centered over the Mid-Mississippi Valley.

That means afternoon temperatures should continue reaching the middle and upper 90s each day, with occasional readings near 100 degrees.

The bigger question later this week will be humidity.

Gulf moisture will gradually increase, potentially pushing dewpoints higher Wednesday through Friday. Exactly how high they climb remains uncertain.

Our southwest winds will continue producing some drying as air descends from the Ozarks. We are also late enough in the growing season that vegetation is not releasing as much moisture into the atmosphere as it did earlier this summer.

Those two factors could keep humidity somewhat lower than some computer models currently suggest.

That matters because the difference between a dewpoint of 66 and 72 degrees can make a substantial difference in the heat index when actual temperatures are already in the upper 90s.

COULD THE HEAT ADVISORY BE UPGRADED?

It is possible.

Current forecasts produce pockets of heat index values above 105 degrees later this week.

If confidence increases that those values will actually occur, portions of the region could eventually require an Extreme Heat Warning.

On the other hand, if southwest winds keep dewpoints lower than currently forecast, heat index values may remain closer to 100 degrees and the Heat Advisory would likely remain appropriate.

Either way, this is significant heat.

Whether the heat index reaches 101 or 106 degrees does not change the basic precautions you should be taking.

Drink plenty of water throughout the day, not just when you begin feeling thirsty. Take frequent breaks if you are working outdoors. Wear lightweight clothing. Check on elderly family members, friends, and neighbors.

And please remember your pets. Fresh water and shade are essential, and pavement can become dangerously hot during afternoons like these.

Never leave children or animals inside a parked vehicle. Temperatures inside a vehicle can become deadly within minutes.

ANY RELIEF?

There are some hints that we could eventually get a little relief toward the end of next weekend.

Some guidance suggests a backdoor cold front could approach from the northeast and push the hottest portion of the air mass farther west.

The problem is that most of our guidance currently keeps the ridge and heat in place.

So while I would love to tell you there is a strong cold front waiting just beyond Friday, I cannot do that yet.

For now, plan on the heat continuing through the work week and potentially into at least part of next weekend.

THE BOTTOM LINE

A Heat Advisory is in effect for the entire First Warn Weather coverage area through Friday.

Monday and Tuesday will bring widespread upper 90s across central Missouri, the St. Louis metro, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois. A few locations could reach 100 degrees.

Heat index values will generally peak around 100 degrees each afternoon.

Very little changes Wednesday through Friday. In fact, increasing humidity could push heat index values even higher later in the week. If values above 105 degrees become more widespread, portions of the region could eventually require an upgrade to an Extreme Heat Warning.

The most important part of this forecast is the duration.

This is a prolonged heat event, not a one-afternoon problem.

Take care of yourself. Check on your neighbors. Give outdoor workers a little extra patience. Keep plenty of water available for your animals. And if you have to spend extended periods outside, give yourself more breaks than you normally would.

Monday is also the final day of meteorological summer.

September begins Tuesday.

Apparently the atmosphere did not get the memo.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

Southwest Illinois

South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.

First Warn Weather: First. Accurate. Trusted.
